text.text: SCN1A, the most prominent gene for epilepsy, encodes the pore-forming subunit of the voltage-gated sodium channel, Na V 1.1.

Loss-of-function variants reduce Na V 1.1 activity in inhibitory neurons leading to hyperexcitability; they are associated with a spectrum of epilepsies, from self-limited phenotypes in genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus, to the prototypic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, Dravet syndrome.
Thousands of SCN1A missense variants have been identified, but determining pathogenicity using ACMG criteria can be challenging.
Currently, 48% of missense SCN1A variants in ClinVar are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS).
We aimed to provide functional evidence to inform variant classification using a highthroughput automated patch-clamp assay.
We validated our assay using 27 true pathogenic SCN1A variants and 25 true benign variants.
The results show that 17/27 true pathogenic variants from patients with Dravet syndrome showed severe reductions in current density, precluding gating analysis.
Of the remaining ten true pathogenic variants, seven showed an increased voltage difference between the midpoints of activation and inactivation (V 0.5diff ).
Current density and V 0.5diff were combined within a graded Bayesian framework to derive a functional log-likelihood ratio reflecting the magnitude of loss of function.
We then applied our validated assay to 16 SCN1A missense variants detected in an Australian cohort: three likely pathogenic, one likely benign and 12 VUSs.
These variants occurred in 31 individuals from 16 families with a broad phenotypic spectrum, including four individuals with Dravet syndrome who carried p.Ser243Phe, p.Met973Val or p.Lys1911Glu.

variants showed loss of function: p.Ser243Phe had reduced current density, whereas p.Met973Val and p.Lys1911Glu had abnormal V 0.5diff despite current density within the normal range.
Of these 16 variants, ten have combined functional scores consistent with abnormal functional evidence.

Combining our functional evidence with ACMG criteria, our findings changed the classification of eight of 16 variants (50%), with six of 12 VUS reclassified as likely pathogenic and two of three likely pathogenic variants upgraded to pathogenic.

We show that calibrated automated patch-clamp assays can provide actionable functional data to enable the interpretation and reclassification of SCN1A variants and inform clinical care, allowing therapeutic optimisation and facilitating access to genetic therapies.

SCN1A encodes the pore-forming subunit of the Na V 1.1 voltage-gated sodium channel, which is predominantly expressed in inhibitory GABAergic interneurons. 1 Loss-of-function (LOF) of Na v 1.1 2 reduces inhibitory signalling, which leads to hyperexcitability of the central nervous system. 1, 3 Pathogenic LOF variants in SCN1A underpin a spectrum of epilepsies, ranging from developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs) such as Dravet syndrome, [2] [3] [4] [5] to genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+). [6] [7] [8] Dravet syndrome, the prototypic DEE, is caused by pathogenic LOF variants in SCN1A in more than 90% of patients. 9 By contrast, GEFS+ is a clinically heterogeneous, autosomal dominant familial epilepsy encompassing a spectrum of epilepsy phenotypes, with febrile seizures as a hallmark; notably, only 19% of GEFS+ families harbour pathogenic SCN1A variants. 8 Variant pathogenicity is determined in accordance with the guidelines established by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) and the Association for Molecular Pathology (AMP), 10 which classify genetic variants as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, variants of uncertain significance (VUS), likely benign or benign.

Whole-cell patch clamp experiments were performed in 384-well plates using the SyncroPatch 384PE (Nanion Technologies, Munich, Germany) APC system.
A single voltage protocol was designed to enable measurement of current density and voltage-dependence of activation and inactivation.
For each sweep, the voltage was held at -120 mV for 200 ms, then stepped up to voltages in the range -100 to +60 mV, increasing in 5 mV intervals, for 100 ms, then stepped up to zero mV for 50 ms.
The current density was taken from the peak current measured at zero mV after holding at -70 mV to mimic the resting membrane potential of neurons.
Each plate contained 32 wells for WT control, 32 wells for each of the ten variants and 32 wells for negative control cells.
Each experiment was repeated once on the same day and two plates were run again on a different day using a different batch of cells to ensure the results were reliable and reproducible.
Data from the APC experiments were analysed using DataControl384 and a customised MatLab script.
Initial quality control (QC) parameters implemented in the DataControl384 software were: minimum seal resistance of 500 MΩ, capacitance value between 2-30 pF, series resistance less than 20 MΩ.

For gating analysis, secondary QC parameters applied were: time to peak at zero mV between 0.5-1.1 ms for current density measurements, and current amplitude cut-offs of 400 pA to 4 nA for voltage-dependence of activation and inactivation to restrict fitting to well-resolved currents while avoiding series resistance voltage error.
Current density was calculated by dividing the inward sodium current of a cell by its capacitance.
The variants were normalised to the mean of the WT of their respective plate to account for variability across plates.

text.text: The benign reference set comprised the 25 true benign variants together with WT (n = 26), and the pathogenic reference set comprised the 27 true pathogenic variants.
Probability densities of the functional score were estimated separately for each reference set by Gaussian kernel density estimation.

Because the two reference distributions do not overlap (benign, S = 23.3-31.8; pathogenic, S = 34.2-50.0), class-specific bandwidths produce an LLR curve that rises almost discontinuously across the unsampled interval between them, assigning the maximum attainable evidence strength to every reference variant.
A single bandwidth was therefore derived by Silverman's rule of thumb from the pooled benign and pathogenic scores (h = 2.82) and applied to both densities.
This represents deliberate smoothing relative to the classspecific values (h = 1.07 for benign and 0.58 for pathogenic) and was adopted to yield a conservative calibration.
Thresholds were reported only within the score interval spanned by the reference variants (S = 23.3-50.0), so that no evidence was assigned by extrapolation beyond values supported by the assay.
For each functional score, the likelihood ratio of pathogenicity was calculated as the ratio of the estimated pathogenic density to the estimated benign density and expressed as log 10 LR.

Here, we present a calibrated APC assay that provides functional data for SCN1A variants to inform reclassification of VUS based on two parameters: (1) peak current density quantified at zero mV and (2) gating defects using the voltage difference between the midpoints of activation and inactivation (V 0.5diff ).

text.text: The advantage of merging V 0.5 activation and inactivation is that while a slight hyperpolarising shift in activation or depolarising shift in inactivation may not place the variant outside the normal range, the V 0.5diff allows us to simplify the interpretation of gating parameter changes.
There is great utility in the design of such a parameter to distinguish between LOF and GOF.
This is particularly useful for genes where information about variant function has serious treatment implications, such as SCN1A and the need to avoid sodium channel blockers in LOF disorders.
However, further validation for GOF pathogenic variants is required to measure GOF-specific parameters, such as persistent sodium current.

Dravet syndrome is typically associated with severe SCN1A LOF, although other genes have been implicated in rare individuals with Dravet syndrome. 39 In our set of 27 true pathogenic SCN1A variants from Dravet patients, most showed moderate-to-severe reductions in current density, while a minority fell within the normal current range and were identifiable as LOF only via abnormal V 0.5diff , indicating gating defects.

text.text: While we use variants of known pathogenicity to determine the sensitivity and specificity of our assay, the single-cell measurements do not allow us to examine variant function as part of a neuronal network.
Due to these limitations, caution must be exercised when applying functionally normal readouts from our assay to a clinical setting.

As a result, we did not apply normal function evidence (BS3) for variants that do not show a LOF phenotype, as outlined in ClinGen's criteria for classifying neuronal sodium channel variants. 19 Finally, this assay is applicable only to LOF phenotypes since the calibration used SCN1A variants from patients with Dravet syndrome, and cannot be applied to GOF SCN1A variants.

text.text: We have validated an APC assay for SCN1A missense variants to detect LOF variants on 25 true benign and 27 true pathogenic variants.
The assay was employed to evaluate variant function in patients with epilepsy and febrile seizures.

Our functional studies have a 50% yield in variant reclassification, with 6/12 VUS reclassified as likely pathogenic and 2/3 likely pathogenic variants upgraded to pathogenic, translating directly to clinical diagnosis and facilitating targeted therapy.

To fully realise the benefits of our APC assay, work should be undertaken in close collaboration with research teams, clinical staff and testing laboratories to ensure patients obtain a definitive genetic diagnosis sooner when they have variants with abnormal function. 13 Figure legends    moderate reductions in current density (coloured as per Fig 3).
